elements.quote: This systematic review assesses the scientific evidence regarding the effectiveness of organisational-level workplace mental health interventions on stress, burnout, non-clinical depressive and anxiety symptoms, and wellbeing in construction workers.
elements.reason: The abstract (Objectives) explicitly identifies the report as a systematic review.

elements.quote: This systematic review assesses the scientific evidence regarding the effectiveness of organisational-level workplace mental health interventions on stress, burnout, non-clinical depressive and anxiety symptoms, and wellbeing in construction workers.
elements.reason: The abstract gives an explicit statement of the main objective/review question (assessing effectiveness of organisational-level interventions on specified outcomes in construction workers).

elements.quote: Eligibility criteria were randomized controlled trials (RCTs), cluster randomized controlled trials (cRCTs), controlled or uncontrolled before- and after studies published in peer-reviewed journals between 2010 and May 2022 in five databases (Academic Search Complete, PsycInfo, PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science). Outcomes were stress, burnout and non-clinical depression and anxiety symptoms, and wellbeing (primary) and workplace changes and sickness absenteeism (secondary).
elements.reason: The abstract/methods text specifies the main inclusion criteria (study designs, date and database limits) and the outcomes of interest, serving as the inclusion/exclusion criteria.

elements.quote: Records identified through database searching, May 28, 2020 ... Records identified through updated database searching, May 16, 2022
elements.reason: The PRISMA flow diagram (included with the article's results) lists the information sources (databases) and shows the dates of searches (May 28, 2020 and May 16, 2022).

elements.quote: Quality appraisal was conducted using the QATQS scale, a narrative synthesis was applied.
elements.reason: The methods statement reports the tool used for quality appraisal (QATQS), indicating how risk of bias/quality was assessed.

elements.quote: We conducted a narrative synthesis of the findings from the included studies, structured around the effectiveness of the mental health intervention programmes. Mean differences (pre- and post- intervention) with p-values were reported and adjusted regression coefficients or adjusted Odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals, if available, were tabulated, brought together, and summarized using narrative synthesis. It was not possible to conduct a meta-analysis for the included studies due to the diversity of interventions and outcomes.
elements.reason: The methods for presenting and synthesizing results are specified: narrative synthesis, tabulation of effect estimates, and inability to perform meta-analysis due to heterogeneity.

elements.quote: After applying all exclusion criteria, five articles from four studies were identified as eligible for inclusion in the review ... Total sample size across the four studies was 260 from a variety of occupations within construction.
elements.reason: The results report the total number of included studies (four studies, five articles) and the total number of participants (260), and summarize key study/sample characteristics.

elements.quote: This review identified a low number of studies on this topic with only one study of moderate methodological quality showing a substantial but non-significant decline in sick leave days [73] and no significant effect on general mental health. Results of the remaining 'weak-quality' studies included a significant effect of work redesign in short-term physiological stress parameters... a significant perceived improvement of flow of information after supervisor training [74]; no significant effect on general mental health [75] and no significant effect on a range of psychosocial work factors and on emotional exhaustion [74].
elements.reason: Main outcome results are summarized (effects and significance), but the abstract/results do not provide detailed per-outcome counts of included studies and participants for each specific outcome, so reporting is partial.

elements.quote: It was not possible to conduct a meta-analysis for the included studies due to the diversity of interventions and outcomes.
elements.reason: No meta-analysis was conducted, so reporting a summary estimate and interval is not applicable.
Although some controlled comparisons are described in the paper, there is no explicit statement in the abstract identifying the direction of effect and which group is favored for the comparisons.

The abstract text provided does not briefly summarize important limitations of the included evidence (risk of bias, inconsistency, imprecision); limitations are discussed elsewhere in the paper but not in the abstract evidence available.

The retrieved abstract content does not provide a general interpretation of the results and their important implications; interpretation and implications appear in the discussion but are not present in the abstract material provided.
Although funding information is present in the manuscript (Methods section), there is no evidence that the abstract itself specifies the primary source of funding.
The protocol registration (PROSPERO CRD42020183640) is reported in the methods and materials, but there is no evidence that the abstract provides the register name and registration number.

elements.quote: This systematic review aimed to assess recent scientific evidence on the effectiveness of organisational-level mental health interventions on non-clinical mental health outcomes and mental wellbeing in the construction industry in general and in SMEs in particular. This review identified a low number of studies on this topic with only one study of moderate methodological quality... The evidence found in the four studies was not sufficient to develop specific recommendations for the design of organisational-level mental health promotion programmes in the construction industry and more specifically for SMEs.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes the current state of knowledge (few studies, low-quality evidence, heterogeneous interventions) and highlights important uncertainties (insufficient evidence to make recommendations), fulfilling the requirement to describe the current state and uncertainties.

elements.quote: Develop and evaluate mental health interventions specific to the working situation in the construction sector. Only one study included in this systematic review addressed the specific psychosocial working conditions of construction workers... Tailoring the intervention more specifically to the workplace may be particularly relevant for the construction industry... There is a rich opportunity for scientific effectiveness and process evaluation of existing and future workplace mental health programmes to determine whether they actually result in mental health improvements, which programme elements are the most effective and which approaches can be best implemented into the construction work environment.
elements.reason: The authors explain the importance and need for conducting the review by outlining gaps (e.g. interventions not tailored to construction, lack of robust evaluation) and articulating the need for future research and evaluation, justifying the review's necessity.

No evidence was found in the provided text that discusses existing similar systematic reviews or explains the need for the current review relative to prior reviews; therefore the conditional requirement is not addressed in the supplied evidence.

elements.quote: Develop a programme theoretical framework. An explicit programme theory is necessary with specification of the expected short-term and long-term outcomes at different levels of the organisation, intermediary outcomes, and mechanisms of change to guide the intervention and evaluation and to avoid chance and error strategies. None of the studies included in our systematic review, spelled out such a model;
elements.reason: Although the authors recommend describing mechanisms and programme theory for future work, they report that the included studies did not spell out mechanisms of action; the review itself does not describe a proposed mechanism of action for the interventions, so this conditional item is not fulfilled.

elements.quote: Develop a programme theoretical framework. An explicit programme theory is necessary... None of the studies included in our systematic review, spelled out such a model; only one study took multi-level variations into account by performing multi-level analyses [73].
elements.reason: The authors discuss the value of a logic model and note that none of the included studies provided such a model; the review does not present a logic model itself, so this conditional reporting element is not met in the provided evidence.

elements.quote: The specific review questions are: (1) Are organisational-level mental health programmes effective in reducing stress, burnout, non-clinical depressive and anxiety symptoms, and in enhancing mental wellbeing in construction workers? (2) Are organisational-level mental health programmes effective in reducing stress, burnout, non-clinical depressive and anxiety symptoms and in enhancing mental wellbeing in SME construction workers?
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly states the specific review questions addressing the objectives of the review, phrased as clear questions about the effectiveness of organisational-level mental health programmes in construction workers and in SME construction workers.

elements.quote: The specific review questions are: (1) Are organisational-level mental health programmes effective in reducing stress, burnout, non-clinical depressive and anxiety symptoms, and in enhancing mental wellbeing in construction workers? (2) Are organisational-level mental health programmes effective in reducing stress, burnout, non-clinical depressive and anxiety symptoms and in enhancing mental wellbeing in SME construction workers?
elements.reason: The review questions specify the population (construction workers, SMEs), the intervention type (organisational-level mental health programmes) and the outcomes of interest (stress, burnout, non-clinical depressive and anxiety symptoms, mental wellbeing) but do not present these planned comparisons in an explicit PICO (or similar labeled) format nor explicitly state comparators or detailed planned comparison structure; therefore the requirement for a PICO-formatted statement is only partially met.

elements.quote: Studies were included if they reported organisational-level mental health promotion interventions targeted at workers and/or managers within construction companies. In a staged approach only studies with a control group and with a before- and at least one after measurement post intervention were deemed eligible in the first round of selection as they provide the most robust evidence. These included randomised controlled trials (RCTs), a study design with participants randomly assigned to an intervention group and a control group; cluster randomised controlled trials (cRCT), with groups of participants (e.g., organisations) being randomised to an intervention and a control group, and non-randomised controlled trials. In a second stage, uncontrolled before- and after- designs and uncontrolled quasi-experimental designs were included in the reviews. Complete inclusion and exclusion criteria can be found in Table 1. Primary outcomes included quantitative measurements of aspects of mental health and wellbeing, secondary outcomes included organisational outcomes such as absenteeism, especially if linked to health issues, and changes to the psychosocial work environment.
elements.reason: The manuscript specifies population (workers/managers in construction), eligible study designs (RCTs, cRCTs, non-randomised controlled trials, uncontrolled before-and-after, quasi-experimental), staged inclusion criteria, and primary/secondary outcomes.

elements.quote: The search was performed using five databases on May 28, 2020, and updated on May 16, 2022: Academic Search Complete, PsycINFO, PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science and included studies published in English between January 2010 and May 2022 to reflect intervention efforts in the modern construction workplace. Unpublished 'grey literature' was not included.
elements.reason: The review states date range (Jan 2010–May 2022), language restriction (English), databases searched and excludes grey literature / unpublished reports and specifies publication in peer-reviewed journals elsewhere.

elements.quote: Primary reasons for exclusion at full-text review were ineligible outcomes (n = 14) and ineligible study design (n = 10).
elements.reason: The review explicitly reports exclusions for ineligible outcomes (i.e., outcomes not meeting criteria), but it does not report or distinguish exclusions due to outcome results not being reported (e.g., measured but not reported).

elements.quote: In a staged approach only studies with a control group and with a before- and at least one after measurement post intervention were deemed eligible in the first round of selection ... In a second stage, uncontrolled before- and after- designs and uncontrolled quasi-experimental designs were included in the reviews.
elements.reason: The review describes grouping studies by design/stage (controlled designs first, then uncontrolled designs) but does not clearly specify the groups used in each synthesis nor explicitly link those groups to predefined comparisons in the review objectives.

elements.quote: included studies published in English between January 2010 and May 2022 to reflect intervention efforts in the modern construction workplace. The search strategy aimed at identifying published studies ... Unpublished 'grey literature' was not included.
elements.reason: The manuscript provides rationales for notable restrictions (timeframe to reflect modern workplace interventions; exclusion of grey literature; staged inclusion of study designs because controlled studies provide more robust evidence).

elements.quote: The search was performed using five databases on May 28, 2020, and updated on May 16, 2022: Academic Search Complete, PsycINFO, PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science and included studies published in English between January 2010 and May 2022 to reflect intervention efforts in the modern construction workplace.
elements.reason: Explicit dates when the searches were performed and updated are reported (May 28, 2020 and May 16, 2022).

elements.quote: The search was performed using five databases on May 28, 2020, and updated on May 16, 2022: Academic Search Complete, PsycINFO, PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science and included studies published in English between January 2010 and May 2022...
elements.reason: The names of the bibliographic databases searched are reported, and the date limits for included studies are given, but the search interface/platform and the databases' available coverage dates are not provided.

elements.quote: Both backward and forward citation chaining of all articles included in the full-text review stage were conducted to identify additional studies that may have met the search criteria but were not previously found in the search results.
elements.reason: The authors specify that backward and forward citation chaining was performed on the reference lists of all articles included at full-text review, which indicates the type of reference lists examined.

elements.quote: Both backward and forward citation chaining of all articles included in the full-text review stage were conducted to identify additional studies that may have met the search criteria but were not previously found in the search results.

elements.quote: The search strategy can be found in S1 File.

elements.quote: The search was performed using five databases on May 28, 2020, and updated on May 16, 2022: Academic Search Complete, PsycINFO, PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science and included studies published in English between January 2010 and May 2022 to reflect intervention efforts in the modern construction workplace.
elements.reason: The manuscript reports date(s) of search, databases searched, language limit (English), and date range (Jan 2010–May 2022) with an explicit justification ('to reflect intervention efforts in the modern construction workplace').

elements.quote: The search strategy was developed in an iterative process using the Population, Intervention, Comparison, and Outcome (PICO) framework and in consultation with the subject librarian ... The search strategy was composed of free text and controlled vocabulary terms for workers in the construction industry (e.g., carpenters, labourers, etc.), intervention type (e.g., workplace mental health promotion), and outcomes (e.g., stress, burnout, mental wellbeing, etc.) grouped together using Boolean operators in consultation with the subject librarian.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes use of controlled vocabulary and free-text terms and an iterative development process, but does not cite specific published search approaches or filters nor describe any adaptations of published filters.
No mention is made of using natural-language processing or text-analysis tools to identify or refine search terms in the provided evidence.
There is no information about tools used to translate search strings between sources in the provided text or supplements referenced.

elements.quote: The search strategy underwent review following the PRESS guidelines [68] by a second and independent, subject librarian in the collaborating author's (BA) institution.
elements.reason: The authors report a PRESS review of the strategy (a form of checking), but do not describe formal validation studies or a detailed validation process beyond this peer review.

elements.quote: The search strategy underwent review following the PRESS guidelines [68] by a second and independent, subject librarian in the collaborating author's (BA) institution.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly states the search strategy was peer-reviewed using the PRESS guidelines by an independent subject librarian, fulfilling reporting of peer review of the search.

elements.quote: The search strategy was developed in an iterative process using the Population, Intervention, Comparison, and Outcome (PICO) framework and in consultation with the subject librarian within the lead author's (BAG) institution.
elements.reason: This element applies only when the search structure was not based on PICO. The authors explicitly state the search was developed using the PICO framework, so the conditional item is not applicable.

elements.quote: To ensure adequate understanding and consistency in application of the inclusion and exclusion criteria, a sample of 20 records were selected at random and their titles and abstracts were reviewed and rated as 'eligible for inclusion' or 'not eligible for inclusion' independently by five authors (CL, CO'B, JCS, BG, BA)... Subsequently, two reviewers (CL, CO'B) completed a blinded title and abstract review of a random sample of 25% of records for inclusion... The remaining 75% of records were then screened at the title and abstract level by one reviewer (CL or CO'B). Blind screening of full-text articles was completed by two authors (CL and BG), who agreed on final inclusion and exclusion decisions.
elements.reason: The text specifies how many reviewers participated at each screening stage: five for the 20-record sample, two for a 25% blinded title/abstract sample, one for the remaining 75% title/abstract screening, and two for blinded full-text screening.

elements.quote: a sample of 20 records ... were reviewed and rated ... independently by five authors (CL, CO'B, JCS, BG, BA) with the Rayyan blinding feature enabled. Subsequently, two reviewers (CL, CO'B) completed a blinded title and abstract review of a random sample of 25% of records for inclusion... Blind screening of full-text articles was completed by two authors (CL and BG)...
elements.reason: The text explicitly states reviewers worked independently/blinded for the 20-record sample, the 25% title/abstract sample, and that full-text screening was performed blinded by two authors.

elements.quote: The five authors then met to discuss their inclusion decisions and any discrepancies were discussed until unanimous agreement was reached... Agreement between the reviewers was 98.3% with the discrepancies resolved through discussion and did not require the input of a third reviewer.
elements.reason: The text describes the process used to resolve disagreements: group discussion until unanimous agreement for the five-author sample, and discussion between reviewers to resolve discrepancies for the 25% sample (no third reviewer required).

elements.quote: Where data were missing, incomplete or unclear, requests for additional information were sent to the corresponding study authors by email.
elements.reason: The text reports that authors were contacted by email to obtain additional information when data were missing or unclear, which describes processes to obtain or confirm information from study investigators.

elements.quote: The search ... included studies published in English between January 2010 and May 2022...
elements.reason: The review included only studies published in English, so translation methods for abstracts or full articles for eligibility assessment do not apply.

elements.reason: The authors report use of Rayyan QCRI and its duplicate-detection and blinding features, indicating integration of automation tools into the selection process.

elements.quote: Results were exported into Rayyan QCRI, a software application to facilitate study selection in systematic reviews [70]. Duplicates were eliminated with the use of the Rayyan duplicate detection feature and verified by one reviewer (CL).
elements.reason: No externally derived classifiers are described or identified in the text; only use of Rayyan for duplicate detection and blinding is reported, so the item on externally derived classifiers does not apply.
No evidence of internally derived classifiers, their training, or validation is reported; therefore this item does not apply.
No machine-learning prioritisation tools or screening stopping/prioritisation rules are reported in the provided evidence.
No crowdsourcing platforms or related processes are described in the provided evidence.

elements.quote: Following removal of duplicates, the title and abstract of 1129 records were reviewed for eligibility.
elements.reason: There is no report of previously screened datasets being used to eliminate records; the flow description refers to duplicates removal and standard screening, so this item does not apply.

elements.quote: Data extraction for the articles after full-text review included the following and was independently cross-checked by a third reviewer: 1, author and year; 2, type of study design; ...
elements.reason: The text states data extraction 'was independently cross-checked by a third reviewer' which indicates involvement of at least a third reviewer checking extracted data, but it does not explicitly state how many reviewers collected data from each report (e.g., one, two, or more collectors).

elements.quote: Data extraction for the articles after full-text review included the following and was independently cross-checked by a third reviewer: ...

No methods for translating articles (e.g., use of translators, machine translation, translation verification) are reported in the provided evidence.
The evidence does not specify any software used to extract data from figures (e.g., graph digitizing tools) during data collection.
No decision rules for selecting data from multiple reports or for resolving inconsistencies across reports are described in the provided text.

elements.quote: Outcomes were stress, burnout and non-clinical depression and anxiety symptoms, and wellbeing (primary) and workplace changes and sickness absenteeism (secondary).
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly lists primary outcome domains (stress, burnout, non-clinical depression and anxiety symptoms, wellbeing) and secondary outcome domains (workplace changes, sickness absenteeism).

elements.quote: Follow-up- measurement points ... Immediate; 2 years post intervention; Measurements during traditional work week versus optimized work week; 3-, 6-, and 12-months post intervention
elements.reason: The review reports follow-up/measurement time points for included studies (see Table 2) and data extraction included 'length of follow-up' and 'all assessment times' (text_15). However, the manuscript does not explicitly specify the time frame of measurement mapped to each outcome domain in a comprehensive way, only study-specific follow-up points.

elements.quote: Reported outcomes, that were not specified as primary or secondary outcomes for the purpose of this review were not included in the results table nor the synthesis.
elements.reason: The manuscript states the approach taken regarding which results were sought: only outcomes specified as primary or secondary for this review were included, indicating whether all compatible results were sought.

elements.quote: Reported outcomes, that were not specified as primary or secondary outcomes for the purpose of this review were not included in the results table nor the synthesis.
elements.reason: When not all compatible results were included, the review describes the selection process: outcomes not specified as primary or secondary for the review were excluded from tables and synthesis.
No information or statement is provided in the retrieved evidence about any changes to outcome-domain inclusion, definitions, or importance, nor rationales for such changes.
No information is provided about any changes to processes for selecting results within eligible outcome domains or rationales for such changes.

elements.quote: Outcomes were stress, burnout and non-clinical depression and anxiety symptoms, and wellbeing (primary) and workplace changes and sickness absenteeism (secondary).
elements.reason: The manuscript identifies primary outcomes (mental health and wellbeing measures) and secondary outcomes (workplace changes, absenteeism), indicating which outcomes were considered most important for interpretation; additional rationale linking organisational-level interventions to psychosocial work environment changes is provided in text_13.

elements.quote: Data extraction for the articles after full-text review included the following and was independently cross-checked by a third reviewer: 1, author and year; 2, type of study design; 3, number of participants and demographics, including employment type; 4, number of control participants and demographics (initial and analysed); 5, intervention details; 6, number of sessions and length; 7, type of control; 8, length of follow-up; 9, relevant outcomes; 10, instruments applied to measure outcomes; 11, country; 12, mean and standard deviation of all study groups in the relevant outcomes at all assessment times to be analysed; and 13, size of the organisation(s).
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly lists and defines a comprehensive set of additional variables (items 1–13) that were sought during data extraction.

The paper describes how missing, incomplete or unclear data were handled (requests to study authors; retrieving organisation size from websites/LinkedIn) but does not describe any assumptions made about missing or unclear study information.
No citation or description of a specific tool used to determine which data items to collect is provided in the supplied evidence.

elements.quote: The quality of each included study was appraised using the Quality Assessment Tool for Quantitative Studies (QATQS) scale [71],
elements.reason: The specific risk-of-bias tool and its name (QATQS) are explicitly stated.

elements.quote: which assesses 6 areas: 1, selection bias; 2, design; 3, confounders; 4, blinding; 5, data collection method; and 6, withdrawals and drop-outs.

elements.quote: Results were scored on a scale from 1 to 3, where 1 is considered methodologically strong, 2 moderate and 3 weak and then globally ranked as methodologically 'strong' = no weak ranking, as 'moderate' = one weak ranking, and as 'weak' with two or more weak rankings.
